label: flydubai 1073, a Boeing 737 MAX 8 (A6-FKF), lines up on runway 30R at Dubai International for Tel Aviv, a flight of about three hours.

From 03:54 to 05:16 the open networks hear nothing over Saudi Arabia; this stretch follows Flightradar24's receivers. The aircraft climbs to 34,000 ft at 04:09 and flies on west past Rafha and Sakaka.
Cruise at 34,000 ft over northern Saudi Arabia
Two hours and eleven minutes after take-off, flydubai 1073 cruises west over Saudi Arabia's Al Jawf region at 34,000 ft.
Descent begins; the selected altitude still reads 34,000 ft
At 05:21:09 the aircraft starts down, reaching 2,900 ft/min. The altitude set on the autopilot panel, which the aircraft keeps broadcasting, still reads 34,000 ft: no descent had been selected.
Abrupt pitch changes; the dive steepens

From 05:21:44 the broadcast pressure altitude jumps by up to 1,000 ft within a second while the GPS positions stay smooth, and the ground speed falls from 441 to 377 kt in five seconds: signs of violent pitch changes. The aircraft then dives, turning right.
At 05:22:13, at 27,950 ft and diving at over 20,000 ft per minute, the aircraft drops out of the open networks' reach for nine minutes. Flightradar24's receivers keep hearing it.
It pulls out at about 16,850 ft at 05:22:36 in a hard right turn through north-east, at about 595 kt over the ground: far faster than a 737 normally flies at that height.
Bottom of the dive: 16,850 ft, ~595 kt

Israeli security officials said the emergency stemmed from a confrontation between the two pilots in the cockpit. Passengers described blood in the cockpit. A report that one pilot tried to dive the aircraft deliberately is unconfirmed.
A zoom climb to 21,725 ft at 05:23:23, then down again past 15,000 ft within a minute, turning north-west.
Open networks hear it again: 15,000 ft, squawk 7700
The open networks hear it again at 05:31:26: level at 15,000 ft, heading north-west toward Jordan. The selected altitude now reads 15,000 ft. The transponder code is 7700, a general emergency.

At 05:35:17 the transponder's emergency status changes to unlawful interference, the meaning of code 7500, used for a hijacking. Israel scrambled fighter jets; Israeli officials later said there was no hijacking.
Over Jordan, south of Al-Jafr, the aircraft turns left through 200° at up to 24° of bank. The heading selected on the autopilot panel changes to 100°: back toward Saudi Arabia.
The selected heading turns to 130°, south-east, at 15,000 ft with code 7500 still set.
At 05:53:32 the open networks lose the aircraft for good. Flightradar24's receivers follow it south-east, then south and south-west toward Tabuk, still at 15,000 ft.
At 06:13 the aircraft leaves Flightradar24's ground coverage. After that only satellites heard it, twice in the air: the descent to Tabuk is reconstructed between those fixes.
06:28:37: a satellite hears it 15 nm north-east of Tabuk at 5,475 ft, heading south-south-west at 205 kt, squawking 7700.
The next fix, 15 minutes later, is only 14 nm away: the aircraft flew about three times that distance, and how is not known. It is drawn here as a long right-hand circuit onto runway 31.
Satellite fix: 3.2 nm out on runway 31
06:43:39, the last airborne fix: 3.2 nm out on runway 31's centreline at 3,375 ft, descending 960 ft/min at 185 kt, on a normal 3° glidepath.
It lands on runway 31 at Tabuk at about 06:44:50. The last satellite fix, at 06:58:59, shows it stopped at the airfield's north-west end. flydubai said all passengers were safe.
